blocks.text: All,

The office reopens tomorrow on the normal schedule. The supply room was restocked over the break with toner, legal pads, and file folders; if you take the last of anything, note it on the sheet inside the door. The kitchen refrigerator was emptied before the holiday, so anything left in it is gone.

Last year's closed files are boxed in the file room for off-site storage. The boxes go out Friday, so pull anything you still need before then; the index is taped to the end of the shelf. Conference room bookings for January go on the shared calendar, not by email.
Best
Hollowell Patent Group PLLC

Hollowell Patent Group PLLC is a patent practice. We prepare and prosecute patent applications, manage portfolios once patents issue, and advise clients on the strength and reach of patents held by others, and we keep the firm to that work so that every matter is handled by people who practice nothing else. This overview describes the services we offer, how a matter is run from the first conversation to the last docketed date, and what a client should expect from us in writing.
What we do
The work falls into four service lines. Each is opened, staffed, and billed as its own matter, so that a client can see what is being done, by whom, and on what terms.

items: Preparation and prosecution: drafting specifications and claims from an inventor's disclosure, responding to office actions, conducting examiner interviews, and managing continuation and divisional filings within a family.

Portfolio review and management: periodic reviews organized by patent family, covering what is pending, what has issued, which response dates and maintenance fees fall due, and where the claims have drifted away from the products they are meant to protect.

Freedom-to-operate and validity analysis: privileged memoranda that define their scope at the outset, separate what the record shows from what remains uncertain, and state each conclusion with the qualifications the analysis supports.

Post-grant proceedings: advice on the exposure presented by a petition before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, and preparation of petitions and patent owner responses where a client decides to proceed.

blocks.text: Who the practice is built for

The firm is organized for clients whose value is concentrated in a modest number of technical patent families: medical device companies, university technology licensing offices, and venture-backed hardware companies building a portfolio that a later investor or licensee will examine closely. This overview does not describe the work of any particular client, and the firm will not cite a client's matter in a document of this kind without that client's written consent.
How a matter runs

Every matter begins with a conflicts check and a written engagement letter that states the scope of the work, the basis on which it is billed, and what follows if invoices go unpaid, and no substantive work begins until that letter is signed. Mary Bradley, our Managing Partner, reviews each engagement letter before it is sent and assigns every matter a responsible attorney or agent, so that at any point one named person owns the next deadline.

Routine updates go to clients as short emails that cite the docket number and state what happened, what is due next, and who is responsible for it. Longer work, such as a portfolio review or a freedom-to-operate memorandum, is delivered as a structured written document, and where a client's board needs the portfolio summarized, we prepare a short presentation for that purpose.
Docket control

We treat the docket as the part of the practice that admits no exceptions, because a missed statutory or response date can cost a client rights that later work cannot recover. Sharon Woods, our Docketing Manager, maintains the firm's docket, sends reminder notices in a fixed format to the responsible attorney or agent well ahead of each date, and escalates any reminder that has not been confirmed in writing.

She also reconciles the docket independently against the patent office's own records, which means that a date entered incorrectly at intake is caught by a second, separate check well before the date itself arrives. An unconfirmed date is treated as an open problem until a named person has taken responsibility for it.
How we write

Our opinions are as qualified as the analysis behind them. We will not tell a client that a product does not infringe, or that a patent is invalid, unless the record supports that statement without reservation, and where it does not, the memorandum states what we found, what we could not determine, and what further work would narrow the question.

Every document a client reads identifies the attorneys and agents on the matter by full name and title. Privileged analysis is marked as privileged on its first page, so that its status never has to be inferred.
Opening a matter

A prospective client should begin by sending us the names of every party involved, including any parent company, licensor, or co-owner, so that we can complete a conflicts check before any confidential information is exchanged. Once that check is clear, Mary Bradley will arrange an initial call to define the scope of the first engagement and will send the engagement letter that governs it.
Onboarding record: Richard Henderson, Patent Agent

Richard Henderson joined Hollowell Patent Group a week ago as a Patent Agent in the Prosecution group, and this record sets out where he sits in the practice, what his first period here involves, and what the firm expects of him by the end of it. We are glad to have him, and glad in particular to have an agent whose engineering training runs to mechanical and medical device subject matter, which suits the applications the firm expects to prepare. He joins a small Prosecution group, which means he will see a wider range of the firm's work earlier than he might at a larger practice, and he is expected to say so when a matter outruns what he knows.

Richard reports to Heather Munoz, Partner, who will assign his matters, review his drafts, and be the first person he goes to with a question of scope or strategy. For the first several weeks his work will consist of drafting specifications and claim sets from inventor disclosures, preparing first drafts of office action responses, and sitting in on examiner interviews, with every filing reviewed by Heather Munoz before it goes to the patent office until she is satisfied that a second read is no longer needed. She will also decide when he begins to handle examiner interviews on his own, and that decision will turn on the quality of his interview summaries more than on the number of weeks he has been here.

The docket comes before everything else here: every response date on a matter Richard works is entered and tracked centrally, reminders reach him in a fixed format, and each one is to be confirmed in writing on the day it arrives, since an unconfirmed date is escalated without further notice to him. Where a date cannot be met, he should say so in writing as soon as he knows, to Heather Munoz and to docketing together, without waiting for the next reminder. He should also expect that anything he writes for a client names him and every other attorney or agent on the matter by full name and title, and that any analysis touching validity or infringement is read by a partner before it leaves the firm.

His office, building access, and accounts on the docket and document systems were set up before he arrived, and his conflicts questionnaire and confidentiality acknowledgment are on file. Mary Bradley will meet with him at the end of his first month to review how the work has gone, and before that meeting he should read the firm's drafting and docketing procedures in full and take any questions about them to Heather Munoz.
Hi Sharon,

With the office closed tomorrow for the holiday, I would like next week settled before either of us leaves today. I will be out on Monday morning, so please move our weekly docket review to Tuesday afternoon, which also gives you Monday to log the mail that came in over the break and to check the reminders against it.

Please also hold the conference room for Wednesday morning, when the attorneys meet to go over the January calendar, and make sure the speakerphone is working, since several people will be dialing in. If Tuesday afternoon does not suit you, send me another time today and I will move my own calendar around it.
Sincerely
New hire: Joseph Walker, Associate

Joseph Walker joined the firm last week as an Associate in the Prosecution group, and this record is written as he begins his second week so that the terms of his first period here are set down while they are still current. He comes to us with a stated interest in freedom-to-operate and validity work, and his first assignments will be chosen to give him a grounding in prosecution together with some exposure to that analysis under close review. Freedom-to-operate work is where the firm's writing is read most closely, by clients and in some cases by opposing counsel years later, so it is also where a new associate is given the least latitude at first.

Joseph reports to Heather Munoz, Partner, who assigns his matters and reviews his drafts, and no memorandum or opinion he prepares goes to a client until she has read it and agreed with its conclusions as written. That is not a judgment on his ability, since the firm applies the same review to every opinion on infringement or validity regardless of who drafts it, and he should expect his conclusions to come back with their qualifications tightened more often than loosened.
For the first period, responsibilities are divided as follows:

items: Joseph Walker: complete the conflicts and confidentiality acknowledgments, read the drafting and docketing procedures in full, and confirm every docket reminder in writing on the day it arrives.
Heather Munoz: assign his first matters, review each draft before it is filed or sent, and decide when his work can go out on a lighter review.
Operations: finish setting up his laptop, remote access, and accounts on the docket and document systems.
Mary Bradley: meet with him at the end of his first month to review how the work has gone and whether his assignments should change.

blocks.text: Anything he writes for a client should name him and every other attorney or agent on the matter by full name and title, and any privileged analysis should carry the legend at the top of its first page. If a client asks him for a view on infringement or validity before that review is complete, the answer is that the firm will respond in writing once the analysis has been reviewed. His next step is to sit down with Heather Munoz this week and agree on his first assignment, once the acknowledgments above are signed and returned.
Ashley Williams: onboarding

Ashley Williams joined the firm last week as a Patent Agent in the Prosecution group, and she reports to Heather Munoz, Partner, who will assign her matters and review her work until both of them are satisfied that a lighter review is enough. Her work will center on preparing and prosecuting applications from inventor disclosures, which at this firm means turning a disclosure written for colleagues in a laboratory or an engineering group into claim language that an examiner, and later a licensee, can read without the inventor in the room. Inventors are not always used to a patent office's timelines, and part of her job is to make those timelines plain to them without leaving room for a missed response.
Expectations for the first period

The docket governs her week from the start. Every response date on a matter she works is tracked centrally, reminders arrive in a fixed format, and each one is to be confirmed in writing on the day it arrives, because an unconfirmed date is escalated without further notice. When she writes to inventors, her notes should be courteous and should leave no doubt about what is needed, with the response date stated in the opening lines and repeated at the end.

For the first several weeks, every draft she prepares, whether an application, a claim amendment, or an office action response, goes to Heather Munoz for review before it is filed, and Heather Munoz will narrow that review to spot checks once the drafts no longer need more. Anything a client will read should name each attorney and agent on the matter by full name and title, and her technical drafts should carry headings that follow the claim structure, so that a reviewer can match each section to the claims it supports.
Logistics

Her laptop, remote access, and accounts on the docket and document systems are in place, and her conflicts and confidentiality acknowledgments are on file. The firm's drafting procedures and response formats are in the shared practice folder, and she should read them before her first draft goes to review. Mary Bradley will meet with Ashley at the end of her first month to review how the work has gone, and before then her next step is to complete the docketing walkthrough this week, so that she has seen how a date moves from intake to reminder before she is responsible for one.
